options.D: Assuming the bias is not a real problem, even though the manager is the one who first noticed the pattern

explanation: Recognizing and overcoming bias means noticing the pattern in one's own judgment and then applying the same written criteria to every resume, regardless of where a candidate went to school. Trusting the favorable feeling as genuine cultural fit accepts the bias rather than questioning it, and removing university names only for already-favored candidates would apply the fix selectively instead of consistently. Assuming the bias isn't a real problem because no one else has mentioned it ignores that the manager has already noticed the pattern personally.

performanceIndicator: Recognize and respond to ethical dilemmas
question: An employee overhears a manager instructing a coworker to leave a product defect out of a customer-facing report. Which response best demonstrates recognizing and responding to this ethical dilemma?

options.A: Raising the concern with the manager or an appropriate channel rather than staying silent
options.B: Ignoring what was overheard since it wasn't said directly to the employee
options.C: Mentioning it to other coworkers without raising it through any formal channel
options.D: Waiting to see whether the customer eventually discovers the defect on their own before deciding what to do

explanation: Recognizing and responding to an ethical dilemma means raising the concern through an appropriate channel rather than staying silent about what was overheard. Ignoring it because it wasn't said directly to the employee, mentioning it only informally to coworkers, and waiting to see if the customer discovers the defect on their own all avoid actually addressing the concern.

performanceIndicator: Recognize and respond to ethical dilemmas
question: A sales associate is asked by a manager to describe a product's return policy to a hesitant customer in a way that is technically true but likely to leave the customer with a misleading impression of how easy returns actually are. Which response best demonstrates recognizing and responding to this ethical dilemma?

options.A: Following the manager's exact wording since it is technically accurate
options.B: Avoiding the customer's question about returns entirely
options.C: Describing the return policy in the same misleading way, even though it means privately promising never to do it again after this one time
options.D: Describing the return policy clearly and accurately, even if it makes the sale less certain

explanation: Recognizing and responding to this ethical dilemma means describing the return policy accurately even when a misleading version would make the sale easier, which is what giving the customer a clear, accurate description does. Following the manager's exact wording because it's technically true still leaves the customer with a false impression. Avoiding the customer's question entirely dodges the dilemma rather than resolving it, and describing the policy misleadingly just once, while privately resolving not to repeat it, still misleads this particular customer.

question: A coworker mentions, visibly upset, that they were passed over for a promotion they had been counting on. Which response best demonstrates empathy?

options.A: Acknowledging how disappointing that must feel and giving the coworker space to talk if they want to
options.B: Immediately listing reasons the decision was probably fair
options.C: Changing the subject to avoid making the moment awkward
options.D: Telling the coworker to quickly focus on the next opportunity instead of dwelling on it

explanation: Empathy means acknowledging how the other person likely feels and giving them room to express it, which is what recognizing the disappointment and offering space to talk does. Listing reasons the decision was probably fair, changing the subject, and telling the coworker to simply move on all minimize the coworker's feelings instead of acknowledging them.

question: A teammate misses an important deadline and is visibly stressed, apologizing repeatedly during a team meeting. Which response best demonstrates empathy?

options.A: Reassuring the teammate that missing deadlines happens to everyone occasionally and it isn't worth feeling bad about at all
options.B: Pointing out in the meeting exactly how the missed deadline affected everyone else's work
options.C: Ignoring the apology and moving directly to the next agenda item
options.D: Acknowledging the teammate's stress and asking what support would help them going forward

explanation: Empathy means acknowledging what the teammate is feeling and asking how to help, which is what recognizing the stress and offering support does. Reassuring them that missing deadlines doesn't matter dismisses their genuine feelings rather than acknowledging them, pointing out the impact on everyone else adds to the pressure instead of addressing it, and ignoring the apology entirely fails to acknowledge the teammate at all.

question: A team lead just rolled out a new weekly reporting process and wants to know how well it's actually working for the team. Which action best demonstrates soliciting feedback?

options.A: Assuming the process works well since no one has complained
options.B: Asking only the two most vocal team members for their opinion
options.C: Sending every team member a company-wide survey containing only yes-or-no questions about the new process
options.D: Asking each team member open-ended questions about what is and isn't working

explanation: Soliciting feedback means actively asking specific, open-ended questions of the people using the new process, not assuming silence means approval. Assuming things are fine because no one has complained, asking only the most vocal members, and using yes-or-no questions all fail to gather real, detailed input from the team.

question: After finishing a big project, a team lead wants to understand what could be improved for next time. Which action best demonstrates soliciting feedback?

options.A: Reviewing the project results alone and drawing conclusions without asking the team
options.B: Holding a debrief and directly asking each team member what they would do differently
options.C: Assuming the project went well since it was delivered on time
options.D: Sending a brief thank-you message to the team without asking any questions about how the project actually went

explanation: Soliciting feedback means directly asking the team what could be done differently, which is what holding a debrief and asking that question accomplishes. Drawing conclusions alone, assuming the project went well simply because it was on time, and sending a thank-you message with no actual questions all fail to gather the team's honest input.

question: A marketing associate needs a specific software license to complete an upcoming project, but a manager has been slow to respond to earlier informal requests. Which action best demonstrates assertiveness?

options.A: Continuing to wait for the manager to eventually notice the earlier requests, even as the project deadline gets closer
options.B: Scheduling a direct conversation with the manager to restate the need and deadline
options.C: Complaining about the delay to coworkers instead of the manager
options.D: Purchasing the software personally without telling the manager

explanation: Assertiveness means clearly and directly restating a need to the person who can act on it, which is what scheduling a direct conversation with the manager does. Continuing to wait for the earlier requests to be noticed, complaining to coworkers instead of the manager, and buying the software personally without telling the manager all avoid directly and clearly communicating the need.

question: An associate disagrees with a decision made in a meeting they weren't invited to but that directly affects their project's timeline. Which action best demonstrates assertiveness?

options.A: Sending a lengthy email to the entire department explaining general concerns about how decisions get made without addressing the specific timeline impact
options.B: Staying quiet about the disagreement since the associate wasn't part of the meeting
options.C: Requesting a brief meeting with the decision-makers to explain the specific impact on the timeline
options.D: Complaining to coworkers about the decision without raising it with the decision-makers

explanation: Assertiveness means raising a specific, well-defined concern directly with the people who made the decision, which is what requesting a brief meeting to explain the timeline impact accomplishes. Sending a broad email about general concerns to the whole department, without addressing the specific timeline issue, dilutes the actual point. Staying quiet because of not being in the original meeting, and complaining to coworkers instead of the decision-makers, both avoid raising the concern where it can actually be addressed.

question: Two shift leads disagree sharply about how to handle a recurring customer complaint, one wants to offer a full refund every time and the other wants to deny all such refunds outright. Which approach best demonstrates conflict-resolution skills?

options.A: Letting whichever shift lead is more senior make the final call without further discussion
options.B: Scheduling separate individual conversations with each shift lead to hear their concerns before ever bringing them together
options.C: Avoiding the issue until a customer complaint forces an immediate decision
options.D: Bringing both shift leads together to agree on a consistent, policy-based response between the two extremes

explanation: Conflict-resolution skills mean bringing both parties together to reach a consistent middle-ground response, which is what getting the two shift leads to agree on a policy-based approach between their two extremes accomplishes. Letting seniority decide skips resolving the actual disagreement, and avoiding the issue until a complaint forces a decision lets the conflict resurface under pressure. Meeting with each shift lead separately, without ever bringing them together, can surface each person's concerns but never actually resolves the disagreement between them.

question: A newly promoted supervisor has the authority to approve or deny requested time off. Which use of that authority best demonstrates using power appropriately?

options.A: Approving requests only from employees who are personal friends
options.B: Applying the same clear criteria to every time-off request regardless of who is asking
options.C: Denying all requests during the supervisor's first month to establish authority
options.D: Reminding employees during every interaction that the supervisor has final say, regardless of how routine or minor the request is

explanation: Using power appropriately means applying the same clear standard to every request, regardless of personal relationships. Approving requests only from friends favors personal connections over fairness, denying all requests just to establish authority misuses the position, and constantly reminding employees of final say emphasizes control rather than fair use of the authority.

question: A project lead outranks no one on the team but needs a teammate from another department to prioritize a shared deadline over that teammate's own manager's requests. Which approach best demonstrates using power appropriately?

options.A: Building the case for cooperation through the shared goal and relevant expertise
options.B: Implying to the teammate that their own manager will be informed if the requested cooperation is not provided quickly enough this week
options.C: Waiting for the teammate to volunteer help without ever directly asking
options.D: Escalating to a manager immediately without first making a direct request

explanation: Using power appropriately without formal authority means building genuine cooperation through the shared goal and relevant expertise, which is what making the case for cooperation on those grounds accomplishes. Implying that a manager will be informed if cooperation isn't quick uses an indirect threat rather than earned influence. Waiting for the teammate to volunteer without ever directly asking is passive rather than an appropriate use of the influence available, and escalating immediately without a direct request skips trying to resolve it directly first.

performanceIndicator: Use social media to solicit ideas
question: A company wants fresh ideas for a new product flavor. Which action best demonstrates using social media to solicit ideas?

options.A: Posting the company's finalized flavor decision on social media along with an explanation of how it was chosen
options.B: Posting a poll on social media asking followers to suggest and vote on new flavor ideas
options.C: Emailing a printed suggestion form to a small internal focus group
options.D: Announcing the new flavor exclusively through an in-store flyer

explanation: Using social media to solicit ideas means directly inviting the audience to contribute and vote on options, which is what a poll asking followers to suggest and vote on flavors accomplishes. Posting a decision that has already been finalized doesn't solicit anything, and an internal focus group or an in-store flyer don't use social media to gather broader input.

performanceIndicator: Use social media to solicit ideas
question: A nonprofit wants community input on which cause its next campaign should support. Which action best demonstrates using social media to solicit ideas?

options.A: Deciding internally and announcing the cause through a press release
options.B: Posting a single general statement on social media asking followers to support the nonprofit's mission overall
options.C: Creating a social media post inviting followers to comment with which cause matters most to them
options.D: Mailing a printed survey to donors from the previous five years

explanation: Using social media to solicit ideas means specifically inviting followers to share their own input, which is what asking followers to comment with which cause matters most does. Deciding internally and announcing the choice, posting a general statement without asking a specific question, and mailing a printed survey all fail to actively solicit ideas through social media.

performanceIndicator: Use social media to solicit ideas
question: A regional retailer wants to gather ideas for improving its loyalty program but has a limited marketing budget for formal research. Which approach best demonstrates using social media to solicit ideas?

options.A: Hiring an outside research firm to conduct in-depth customer interviews
options.B: Running a social media post asking loyalty members to comment with one change they'd like to see
options.C: Waiting for customers to volunteer suggestions without prompting them
options.D: Mailing a lengthy printed survey to every loyalty member's home address and waiting for responses to arrive

explanation: Using social media to solicit ideas on a limited budget means posting a low-cost, direct prompt asking members to share a specific suggestion, which is what asking loyalty members to comment with one change accomplishes. Hiring an outside research firm for in-depth interviews is not a low-budget, social-media-based approach. Waiting for customers to volunteer suggestions without prompting them gathers little input, and mailing a lengthy printed survey to every member's home is both costly and does not use social media at all.

question: A store's remodeling crew needs to see, on one page, which tasks overlap and how many days each one runs across the eight-week schedule. Which tool displays that?

options.A: A monthly expense summary
options.B: An organization chart for the crew
options.C: A supply requisition log listing each vendor order
options.D: A Gantt bar chart

explanation: A Gantt bar chart lays each task on a time axis as a bar, so overlapping work and the duration of every task are visible at once. The other three are real project records, but an expense summary, an organization chart and a requisition log show money, reporting lines and orders rather than the timing of the work.

question: A product-launch team must find out which delays would push the launch date back and which would be absorbed without moving it. Which tool answers that?

options.A: A weekly time sheet for each team member
options.B: A critical-path diagram of the task dependencies
options.C: A project status newsletter
options.D: A team roster list

explanation: A critical-path diagram maps how tasks depend on one another and shows which chain of work sets the finish date, so a delay on that chain moves the launch and a delay elsewhere does not. The other three are genuine project documents, but time sheets, status newsletters and rosters record hours, updates and people rather than task dependencies.

question: Northline Outfitters opens a pop-up shop in six weeks. Visual merchandising cannot begin installing until the custom fixtures arrive, and the fixture order has just slipped four days. The project manager needs to know whether the opening date itself is now at risk.

options.A: A responsibility matrix naming an owner for each install task
options.B: A weekly status report circulated to every department after each install shift
options.C: A budget variance report for the quarter
options.D: A network diagram of task dependencies and float times

explanation: A network diagram shows which tasks feed the install and how much float each one carries, so the manager can see whether four lost days are absorbed by slack or push the opening. A responsibility matrix assigns ownership but says nothing about timing. A weekly status report arrives after the fact and reports progress rather than schedule risk. A budget variance report tracks money, and the problem here is time, not cost.

question: Ridgeline Sports Supply's year-end records show cost of goods sold of $960,000, beginning inventory at cost of $120,000, and ending inventory at cost of $30,000. What was the company's inventory turnover for the year?

options.A: 32 inventory turns for the year
options.B: 8.0 inventory turns for the year
options.C: 12.8 inventory turns for the year
options.D: 6.4 inventory turns for the year

explanation: Average inventory is ($120,000 + $30,000) / 2 = $75,000, and $960,000 / $75,000 = 12.8 turns. The other three come from dividing by the ending inventory alone, by the beginning inventory alone, or by the two inventory figures added together instead of averaged.

question: Willowmere Outdoor's tent department turned its inventory 6.0 times last year and 4.0 times this year. Cost of goods sold for the department was the same in both years. What does the change tell the buyer?

options.A: Average inventory has risen relative to cost of goods sold, tying up cash
options.B: Suppliers shortened lead times, so replacement stock now arrives before shelves empty
options.C: The gross margin earned on each tent sold has widened
options.D: Cost of goods sold has doubled since last year

explanation: Turnover is cost of goods sold divided by average inventory. With cost of goods sold flat, a drop from 6.0 to 4.0 can only come from a larger average inventory, which means more cash sitting in stock. Shorter supplier lead times would normally let the buyer hold less stock and raise turnover, not lower it. Gross margin is a pricing measure and does not appear in the turnover calculation at all. Cost of goods sold is stated as unchanged, so the fourth option contradicts the scenario.

question: Fernwood Home Goods plans August sales of $120,000 and a planned end-of-month inventory of $150,000. Beginning-of-month stock is $145,000, and merchandise already ordered for August delivery totals $20,000. How much may the buyer still spend on August merchandise?

options.A: $95,000 in open-to-buy for August
options.B: $85,000 in open-to-buy for August
options.C: $5,000 in open-to-buy for August
options.D: $105,000 in open-to-buy for August

explanation: Planned purchases are $150,000 + $120,000 - $145,000 = $125,000, and subtracting the $20,000 already on order leaves $105,000. The other three come from reversing the beginning and ending inventory figures, from deducting the merchandise on order a second time, and from taking only the change between beginning and ending stock.

question: Three weeks into the month, a housewares buyer at Copperfield Stores has spent her entire open-to-buy for the period. A vendor then offers a fast-selling item that the floor team says would sell out in days. Company policy holds buyers to the monthly plan.

options.A: Charge the purchase to the store's operating budget
options.B: Negotiate a lower unit cost with the vendor so the total order fits the plan
options.C: Cancel a slower-selling order to free dollars
options.D: Wait until next month's plan releases new purchase dollars

explanation: Open-to-buy measures unspent planned purchase dollars, so the only way to fund a new order inside the month is to release dollars already committed to weaker merchandise. Charging merchandise to the operating budget mixes expense dollars with inventory dollars and hides the overspend rather than solving it. Negotiating a lower cost helps but the buyer has zero dollars left, so a cheaper order is still an order she cannot place. Waiting for next month gives up the selling weeks that made the item attractive.

performanceIndicator: Calculate sell-through rate and stock-to-sales ratio
question: A boutique owner wants to know what share of the units she received in a shipment have been bought during the first four weeks on the floor. Which measure gives her that share?

options.A: Gross margin return on inventory investment
options.B: Stock-to-sales ratio
options.C: Inventory turnover for the season
options.D: Sell-through rate

explanation: Sell-through rate divides units sold by units received, so it reports exactly what portion of a delivery has moved in a given stretch of time. The other three are real merchandising measures, but they compare inventory to profit, to sales volume, and to cost of goods sold rather than to the size of the shipment received.

performanceIndicator: Calculate sell-through rate and stock-to-sales ratio
question: Alder & Vine, a home-fragrance chain, closed March with a stock-to-sales ratio of 5.0 in its candle department against a planned ratio of 3.5. Candle sales for March came in exactly on plan.

options.A: Candle stock on hand ran well above the level the month's sales volume supported
options.B: Candle sales exceeded plan and left the department short of stock
options.C: The candle department's gross margin fell during March
options.D: Candle markdowns were taken too early

explanation: Stock-to-sales ratio compares inventory on hand to sales for the period, so a 5.0 against a planned 3.5 with sales on plan means the numerator, the inventory, is the part that ran high. Sales did not exceed plan, so the second option contradicts the stem. Gross margin is a pricing outcome and is not an input to the ratio. Early markdowns would tend to move stock out and pull the ratio down rather than push it above plan.

question: Riverbend Print Co. allows only employees who have finished the manufacturer's training session to run the laminator. A new associate has not taken the session, and the shift is short-handed with a rush job waiting.

options.A: Decline to run it
options.B: Run it while a trained coworker watches from nearby
options.C: Read the laminator's manual first
options.D: Ask a manager for a waiver

explanation: An equipment policy that restricts operation to trained staff binds the untrained associate no matter how busy the shift is, so declining and handing the job to a qualified operator is the compliant choice. Watching, reading the manual and asking for a waiver all substitute something informal for the required training, which the policy does not permit a supervisor or an associate to trade away.

question: A retailer's marketing team has scheduled a two-day flash sale that is expected to triple traffic. Which step best coordinates the promotion with the store-operations team?

options.A: Post extra signs in store
options.B: Email customers a reminder
options.C: Ask finance to approve the discount
options.D: Share the sale dates and forecast with store staffing

explanation: Giving store staffing the dates and the traffic forecast lets operations schedule enough associates and stock before the event, which is what coordination between the two departments means. Signage and customer email are promotion tasks marketing handles alone, and a finance approval settles the discount rather than preparing the store to serve the crowd.

question: A grocery chain's promotions team and its distribution center repeatedly disagree about when advertised merchandise has to reach the stores. Which practice best prevents the disagreement from recurring?

options.A: A quarterly newsletter
options.B: A monthly report of sales by department manager
options.C: A written job description for buyers
options.D: A shared promotional calendar

explanation: A calendar both departments work from puts ad dates and required delivery dates in one place, so promotions and distribution plan against the same deadlines instead of their own. A newsletter and a sales report communicate after the fact, and a job description defines one role rather than aligning two departments on timing.

question: Larkin Grocers' marketing department books a supplier product demo for the first Saturday of the month. The store's operations manager has already scheduled the annual physical inventory count for that same morning. Both teams find out two days beforehand.

options.A: Ask the supplier to send extra samples
options.B: Meet the operations manager to compare priorities and reset one of the two dates
options.C: Ask store associates to run the demo between inventory counts
options.D: Move the physical inventory to the following week

explanation: Coordination between departments means the two managers resolve the conflict together and agree which activity moves, since each holds authority over its own schedule. Extra samples do not address the double booking at all. Asking associates to work the demo between counts loads two jobs onto the same people and puts the count's accuracy at risk. Moving the inventory unilaterally overrides a decision that belongs to operations, which is the behavior that created the friction.

question: Which practice at a manufacturer most clearly shows that quality has become part of the company's everyday culture rather than one department's assignment?

options.A: Managers audit files monthly
options.B: Inspectors check the last unit shipped
options.C: Workers may stop the line
options.D: Defect reports are filed with the plant manager

explanation: Letting any worker halt production when something looks wrong puts responsibility for quality on everyone on the floor, which is the defining mark of a quality culture. Monthly audits, end-of-run inspection and filing reports upward all leave quality with a manager or an inspector after the work is already done.

question: Brightwater Beverages tells its staff that quality is everyone's job. Which management action would most support that message?

options.A: Train every department in defect review
options.B: Assign defect reviews to a separate inspection team
options.C: Publish a quality slogan
options.D: Add a final inspection step

explanation: Training each department to review defects gives every employee the skill the message asks them to use, so the stated value is backed by capability rather than words. A separate inspection team and an added final inspection both move responsibility to specialists, and a slogan restates the message without changing what anyone does.

question: Staff surveys at a hotel group show that employees notice service problems often but rarely report them, because past reports led to individual employees being disciplined. Management wants reporting to rise.

options.A: Post monthly defect counts by department in the break room
options.B: Treat each reported problem as process data and act on it without naming blame
options.C: Add a manager review step before any guest complaint is logged
options.D: Reward the department with fewest complaints

explanation: Employees stopped reporting because reporting was punished, so the culture changes only when a report becomes information about the process rather than evidence against a person. Posting counts by department keeps the spotlight on who is at fault and adds public pressure. A manager review step before logging puts a filter in front of the very reports management wants more of. Rewarding the fewest complaints pays departments to keep problems quiet, which deepens the original defect.

question: A distribution supervisor is offered a personal gift by a freight carrier that is currently bidding for the company's shipping contract. What is the ethical response?

options.A: Accept it politely
options.B: Accept it and share it with the team
options.C: Decline the gift and disclose the offer to management
options.D: Return it after the bid closes

explanation: Declining and telling management keeps the supervisor free of obligation to a bidder and puts the offer on the record where the company can protect the fairness of the bid. Accepting it privately or sharing it with the team still creates the obligation, and holding the gift until the bid closes leaves the influence in place during the decision that matters.

question: Quality logs at a bottling plant show that one batch ran slightly below the fill weight printed on the label. The plant manager asks the line lead to enter the labeled weight in the log so the shipment can leave on schedule.

options.A: Record the labeled weight
options.B: Rerun the batch now
options.C: Record the measured weight and report it
options.D: Ship the batch and note the difference next month

explanation: Operating records have to reflect what the equipment actually produced, so entering the measured weight and raising it with management is the honest action even under schedule pressure. Recording the labeled weight falsifies the log, rerunning a batch is a production decision that does not address the false entry being requested, and deferring the note to next month lets an inaccurate record stand while the product ships.

question: Silverpine Foods holds its vendors to a written supplier code of conduct. An audit finds that one low-cost ingredient supplier has quietly subcontracted part of its work to a facility the code would not approve. The buying season opens in three weeks.

options.A: Continue the current order and add the subcontracting question to next year's audit
options.B: Notify the supplier of the violation and require a corrective plan
options.C: Cancel all orders with the supplier this week
options.D: Ask the buyer to find a second source

explanation: A supplier code is enforceable only if a documented breach draws a documented response, so telling the supplier and demanding a corrective plan applies the standard while keeping the season's supply intact. Continuing the order and deferring the issue a year treats the code as advisory. Cancelling everything immediately skips the remedy step the code itself contemplates and leaves the company short three weeks out. Finding a second source is prudent planning but leaves the current violation unanswered.

question: Ridgeway Market has finished remodeling its checkout area. The store manager must now decide whether the remodel did what the company wanted it to do. Which step best supports that decision?

options.A: Survey the crew now
options.B: Count the labor hours used
options.C: Compare outcomes against the original objectives
options.D: Review the vendor's final invoice

explanation: Evaluating a finished project means measuring what it delivered against what it was set up to deliver, so the objectives written at the start are the yardstick. Crew opinions, labor hours and the final invoice each describe one input or cost of the work rather than whether the intended outcome was reached.

question: At the close of a store-fixture rollout, the team meets to record what worked, what went wrong, and what the next rollout should do differently. What is the team producing?

options.A: A revised project scope statement
options.B: A lessons-learned review
options.C: A work breakdown
options.D: A resource plan covering the next fiscal quarter

explanation: A lessons-learned review is the closing document that captures what a completed project taught the organization so later projects can use it. A scope statement, a work breakdown and a resource plan are all planning documents written before or during the work, not records of how the finished work turned out.

question: A regional chain installed self-checkout in 12 stores with two stated goals: cut average wait time by 30 seconds and cut checkout labor hours by 10 percent. Six months on, wait time is down 40 seconds, while labor hours are unchanged because the freed associates were moved to the sales floor. How should the team report the result?

options.A: Met on wait time, missed on labor hours
options.B: The project failed because labor costs did not fall as expected
options.C: The project succeeded, since the reassigned staff now support other store tasks
options.D: The result cannot be judged until a full year passes

explanation: The project carried two measurable goals and the evidence splits between them, so an honest evaluation reports each against its own target. Calling the whole project a failure ignores a wait-time goal that was beaten by ten seconds. Calling it a success because staff were redeployed substitutes a benefit nobody set as a goal for the labor target that was set. Waiting a full year postpones a judgment the stated six-month measures already support.

question: Before a store-opening project begins, the team wants to be able to show afterward whether the project succeeded. What should the team put in place at the start?

options.A: A list of every task and its owner
options.B: Measurable criteria for schedule, cost and scope
options.C: A daily stand-up meeting
options.D: A contingency cash fund

explanation: Success can only be demonstrated later if the standard for it is written down first, in terms that can be measured against the finished work. A task list, a daily meeting and a contingency fund all help the team run the project, but none of them states what result would count as success.

question: A distributor's new routing software was delivered on schedule and under budget, yet six months later the drivers still plan their routes by hand. Which fact matters most in judging whether the project succeeded?

options.A: That it came in under budget
options.B: That it shipped on time
options.C: Whether the intended benefit was achieved
options.D: That the vendor met every milestone in the contract

explanation: A project exists to produce a business result, so success turns on whether the routing improvement the software was bought for actually materialized. Budget, delivery date and vendor milestones measure how well the work was managed and can all be met by a project that changes nothing for the business.

question: Cobalt Home Fitness completed a warehouse-automation project four weeks late and 8 percent over budget. Order-picking errors have since fallen by half, and the investment's payback period is now a year shorter than the plan assumed. The steering committee must record a verdict.

options.A: Judge it successful on benefits while noting the overruns
options.B: Judge it unsuccessful, because the schedule and budget targets set the terms
options.C: Defer any judgment until picking errors hold for a full year
options.D: Judge it successful because it finished

explanation: Schedule and budget measure delivery, while error reduction and payback measure the value the company was buying, and here the value targets were beaten. The honest verdict records both. Declaring the project unsuccessful treats delivery measures as the whole test and discards a shortened payback. Deferring a year ignores results that are already measured. Calling it successful merely because it finished sets no standard at all and would rate every completed project the same way.

question: Harbor Lane Retail wants one record that shows, month by month, how each of its suppliers has done on the measures the company tracks. Which record serves that purpose?

options.A: A file of purchase orders sorted by the order date
options.B: A signed master contract
options.C: A supplier scorecard updated each month
options.D: The current price list

explanation: A scorecard collects the same measures for every supplier period after period, which is what makes performance comparable across suppliers and visible over time. Purchase orders, the master contract and the price list document what was ordered, what was agreed and what things cost, none of which records how the supplier actually performed.

question: A forklift at Cedar Ridge Distribution swerved and came within inches of a worker in the aisle. Nobody was hurt and nothing was damaged. What does a standard accident-reporting procedure call for?

options.A: Report the near miss the same as an injury
options.B: Tell the shift lead verbally at the end of the day
options.C: Log it if it happens again
options.D: File it next quarter

explanation: Accident procedures cover near misses because the same conditions that produced a close call will eventually produce an injury, and only a written report puts those conditions in front of safety staff. A verbal mention leaves no record, waiting for a repeat means the hazard stays in the aisle, and holding the report until next quarter delays the investigation past any useful point.

question: A stockroom associate cuts her hand on a broken pallet band. The cut is bleeding steadily but is not severe. The coworker standing beside her has no first-aid training, the store's trained responder is two aisles away, and the supervisor is on the sales floor.

options.A: Clear the broken banding from the aisle before anyone else is cut
options.B: Get the trained first-aid responder and the supervisor
options.C: Drive the associate to a nearby clinic
options.D: Write the incident report at once so the details are recorded while fresh

explanation: Accident procedure puts trained care and supervisor notification first, and both people the coworker needs are in the building. Clearing the banding addresses the hazard but leaves an injured employee unattended. Driving her to a clinic bypasses the trained responder and the supervisor who must authorize and document the response. The incident report is required, but it is written after the injured employee has been cared for, not instead of it.

performanceIndicator: Explain employee role in expense control
question: A retail associate wants to help hold down the store's operating costs during a slow week. Which everyday habit does that?

options.A: Order backup supplies early
options.B: Print a paper copy of every email for the file
options.C: Turn off unused lights
options.D: Keep the stockroom door propped open

explanation: Utilities are a controllable store expense, and switching off lighting in areas nobody is using lowers that bill without affecting service. Ordering supplies early ties up cash sooner than needed, printing every email spends paper and toner on records already stored, and a propped stockroom door lets conditioned air escape and raises the same utility cost the associate is trying to cut.

performanceIndicator: Explain employee role in expense control
question: Managers at Glenview Hardware tell the staff that a dollar of avoidable expense comes straight out of store profit. Which employee habit best supports that point?

options.A: Reuse shipping cartons for store transfers
options.B: Reorder supplies each week
options.C: Keep a spare set of each supply item in the stockroom
options.D: Work extra hours

explanation: Reusing cartons the store already paid for removes a purchase from the supply budget, which is precisely the kind of avoidable cost an employee controls day to day. Reordering weekly and holding a spare of everything both put more cash into supplies than the store needs on hand, and working extra hours raises payroll, the largest controllable expense of all.

performanceIndicator: Explain employee role in expense control
question: A shift supervisor at Marlow Cafe sees that food-waste cost has climbed for three straight months while sales have stayed flat. Her crew bakes the day's pastries in one large batch at the start of each shift.

options.A: Prepare pastries in smaller batches timed to the store's hourly sales pattern
options.B: Ask the district manager to raise the store's monthly waste allowance
options.C: Discount the pastries left at closing
options.D: Order a cheaper pastry mix from a second supplier

explanation: Waste is the expense the crew actually controls, and baking to the hours when customers buy prevents product from being made that nobody will purchase. Raising the waste allowance changes the budget rather than the waste. Closing discounts recover a little revenue after the loss is already built into the product. A cheaper mix lowers the cost of each wasted pastry but leaves the same number of them in the bin.

question: At Sandpiper Apparel, four managers each name the responsibility that takes most of their week. Which one is describing the operations function?

options.A: Setting the price points for the fall assortment
options.B: Auditing the books
options.C: Scheduling the production line
options.D: Recruiting seasonal sales associates

explanation: Operations covers the day-to-day activities that turn inputs into finished goods, and scheduling the line is exactly that work. Pricing belongs to marketing, auditing to accounting, and recruiting to human resources, which are all separate business functions.

question: Brightleaf Coffee advertises a drink in a customer's hand within three minutes at every store. Traffic is forecast to rise 20 percent next quarter, and the leadership team asks what the operations function should contribute to keeping that promise.

options.A: Raising drink prices during peak hours
options.B: Adding a loyalty program that rewards customers who order ahead on the app
options.C: Running a radio campaign that features the three-minute promise
options.D: Redesigning the drink station's workflow and staffing

explanation: Operations is responsible for how the work gets done, so changing the layout and staffing of the drink station is the function's own lever on service time. Peak pricing is a revenue decision, a loyalty program is a customer-retention program, and a radio campaign promotes the promise rather than delivering it. Each of the other three may be worth doing, but none of them changes how fast a drink is made.

question: What distinguishes a project from the routine work a department performs week after week?

options.A: It uses a written budget plan
options.B: It is carried out by employees from one department
options.C: It is reviewed by senior management
options.D: It has an end date

explanation: A project is temporary work undertaken to produce one specific result, so a defined finish is what separates it from ongoing operations. Routine departmental work can also carry a written budget, sit inside one department and be reviewed by senior management, so none of those three tells the two apart.

question: A newly promoted project manager is asked what her role adds that the individual task owners do not already provide.

options.A: Balancing scope, schedule and cost as one trade-off
options.B: Approving invoices
options.C: Training the staff on new equipment
options.D: Setting the annual budget

explanation: Project management exists to manage the tension among what is delivered, when, and at what cost, since a change to any one of the three moves the other two. Approving invoices, training staff and setting the annual budget are real duties, but each belongs to a functional manager and none of them requires weighing the three constraints against each other.

question: Halfway through a six-store signage rollout, the marketing director asks the project manager to add exterior signs at four of the locations, keeping the same finish date and the same budget. What is the project manager's proper response?

options.A: Accept the request and absorb the extra work by shortening the installation testing
options.B: Decline the request as outside the plan
options.C: Show what the added scope costs in time and money
options.D: Ask each store manager to arrange the exterior signs locally

explanation: Added scope has to be priced in schedule and cost before anyone can decide on it, and presenting that trade-off is the project manager's job rather than accepting or refusing on her own. Absorbing the work by cutting testing hides the cost in quality. A flat refusal ignores that scope changes are legitimate when their impact is understood. Pushing the work to store managers moves the same cost off the project's books without removing it from the company.

question: A furniture plant's purchasing agent switches to a lower-priced lumber supplier whose boards vary noticeably in thickness. What is the likely effect on the plant?

options.A: Output is unchanged
options.B: Machine setup time drops because boards are thinner
options.C: Material cost per unit rises
options.D: Output falls as workers rework boards

explanation: Inconsistent material forces extra sanding, resetting and scrapping, so labor hours buy fewer finished pieces and productivity drops even though the purchase price fell. Output does not stay the same when the input changes, thinner boards do not shorten machine setup, and the stated purchase price is lower rather than higher.

question: A bakery's purchasing clerk places a flour order only after the last bag in the storeroom is opened. Deliveries take three days to arrive. How does this practice affect the bakery's productivity?

options.A: Production stops while the line waits
options.B: Storage costs rise sharply
options.C: Flour quality drops
options.D: The bakery earns a discount for small frequent orders

explanation: Ordering at the moment stock runs out leaves a three-day gap with no material, and idle ovens and idle bakers produce nothing, which is a direct loss of productivity. Storage costs fall rather than rise when inventory is kept this low, waiting to order does not change the flour's quality, and volume discounts reward larger orders, not smaller ones.

question: Two suppliers quote the same unit price for packaging film. Supplier A ships weekly and has a 2 percent defect rate. Supplier B ships monthly, has a 9 percent defect rate, and requires the plant to inspect every roll on arrival. Which reasoning should guide the purchasing decision?

options.A: The two are equivalent because the unit prices match
options.B: Supplier B is better for its lower freight
options.C: Supplier B is better because monthly deliveries reduce receiving paperwork
options.D: Supplier A costs less overall, since fewer defects and inspections free up run time

explanation: Purchasing affects productivity through what the material does on the floor, and defective film plus mandatory inspection consume labor hours that the quoted price never shows. Treating the two as equivalent stops at the invoice. Lower freight and lighter receiving paperwork are real savings but small next to a defect rate more than four times higher and an inspection step on every roll.

question: A specialty retailer has been losing merchandise from the back stockroom, which opens directly onto the delivery dock. On delivery mornings the staff prop the dock door open so carts can move in and out freely, and the dock is out of sight of the sales floor.

options.A: Move the higher-value stock to the sales floor
options.B: Keep the dock door closed and controlled
options.C: Add a camera that records the sales floor's main entrance
options.D: Ask every delivery driver to sign the receiving log before entering the dock

explanation: The propped door is the uncontrolled opening the losses run through, so restoring control of that entry point addresses the cause rather than its symptoms. Moving stock to the sales floor exposes valuable goods to a different loss risk. A camera aimed at the front entrance watches the wrong door. A signed receiving log documents drivers who identify themselves and does nothing about anyone else walking through an open door.

question: A shirt retailer buys from a maker whose only fabric mill closes for two weeks after a flood. What does the supply chain concept predict for the retailer?

options.A: Shirt deliveries slip several weeks later
options.B: Retail shirt prices fall while the mill is closed
options.C: Cotton growers gain sales
options.D: Shirt quality improves

explanation: Each member of a supply chain depends on the one before it, so a stoppage upstream at the mill works its way forward and delays the finished shirts the retailer expects. Reduced supply pushes prices up rather than down, the grower loses an outlet while the mill is idle, and a flood shutdown gives no reason for quality to improve.

question: Which activity in a bicycle company's supply chain takes place furthest upstream, before any of the others?

options.A: Assembling the frames at the factory
options.B: Mining the metal ore
options.C: Shipping bikes to dealers
options.D: Selling finished bikes in the company's own stores

explanation: Upstream means closer to the raw material, and extracting the ore comes before any of it can be milled, assembled, shipped or sold. Assembly, shipping and retail selling all happen after the material has already entered the chain, with retail selling the furthest downstream of the four.

question: Meadowbrook Toys sells through 400 stores that each hold four weeks of safety stock. Its distributor holds six weeks and its factory holds eight. A modest rise in holiday demand at the stores produces an enormous order swing at the factory. What is happening?

options.A: The bullwhip effect building across the chain tiers
options.B: A seasonal sales pattern that repeats at each of the 400 stores in December
options.C: A shortage caused by factory downtime
options.D: A pricing error that raised the toy's cost to distributors

explanation: Each tier orders to cover its own demand plus its own safety stock, so a small change at the store level is amplified as it passes to the distributor and again to the factory. A seasonal pattern would raise demand at every tier by roughly the same proportion instead of magnifying it. No factory downtime appears in the scenario. A pricing error would change what partners pay, not the size of the order swing.

question: A regional bakery and its flour supplier signed an agreement to share weekly forecasts and plan production together. Six months later the bakery still sends its forecast days late, and the supplier quietly keeps building the same safety stock it always held. What most likely explains the outcome?

options.A: The two firms use different accounting calendars for the year
options.B: Neither partner trusts the other's data
options.C: Flour prices moved after the agreement was signed
options.D: The bakery's delivery trucks run on a schedule the supplier's dock cannot meet

explanation: Collaboration only pays off when each partner acts on what the other shares, and both behaviors here show the opposite: one withholds information by sending it late, the other insures against it with stock. Mismatched accounting calendars complicate reporting but not weekly forecasting. A price move changes the cost of flour without explaining why forecasts arrive late. A dock scheduling conflict is a logistics problem that neither the late forecasts nor the extra safety stock would follow from.

question: The manufacturer's manual for a store's floor buffer calls for a pad change every 20 hours of use. The cleaning crew has been changing pads whenever the finish starts to look dull, which works out to about every 35 hours.

options.A: Keep changing the pads by appearance
options.B: Ask the crew to buff faster
options.C: Change the pads on the schedule the manual sets
options.D: Buy a second buffer

explanation: Manufacturer instructions set the intervals the machine was designed and warranted for, so the 20-hour schedule governs even when a worn pad still looks acceptable. Judging by appearance substitutes a guess for the specification, buffing faster does not change how quickly a pad wears, and a second machine adds cost while the same practice continues on both.

question: A new associate at a packaging plant is taught a shortcut for the shrink-wrapper that leaves out one step of its written setup instructions. The coworker teaching him has used that shortcut for years without a problem. What should the associate do?

options.A: Use the coworker's shortcut
options.B: Time both methods over a full week
options.C: Ask another crew
options.D: Load the machine the way the instructions specify

explanation: Written operating instructions are the standard an employee is accountable to, and a step that has not caused trouble yet is still a step the manufacturer included for a reason. Adopting the shortcut, timing the two methods and polling another crew all treat the printed procedure as one option among several rather than the requirement.

question: A convection oven's manual requires a 15-minute cool-down before the interior racks are pulled. During a lunch rush the kitchen lead needs the racks out in five minutes to change the menu over, and the oven's outer shell already feels cool to the touch.

options.A: Remove the racks using heat-proof gloves
options.B: Wait out the cool-down the manual specifies and switch the menu when it ends
options.C: Speed the cool-down with a fan for five minutes and log the change
options.D: Ask the manufacturer's help line to confirm the wait

explanation: The cool-down interval is a specification, and a cool outer shell says nothing about the interior surfaces and heating elements the instruction is written for. Gloves protect skin but do not make the racks safe to move or protect the oven. Logging the shortcut records a departure from the instruction rather than correcting it. Calling the help line to confirm a written instruction spends the same minutes without changing what the manual already states.

question: A stockroom associate needs a carton stored on a shelf about eight feet off the floor. What is the correct safety precaution?

options.A: Climb the shelving with both hands on the uprights
options.B: Use the stockroom's step ladder
options.C: Pull the carton down with a long broom
options.D: Ask for a lift up

explanation: A step ladder is the equipment provided for reaching height safely, and using it keeps the associate stable with the carton controlled. Climbing shelving loads racking that is not built to carry a person, knocking a carton down with a broom sends it falling uncontrolled, and being boosted by a coworker leaves both people off balance.

question: An associate turns into a grocery aisle and finds a puddle of cooking oil on the floor. The mop station and warning cones are two aisles away, and customers are shopping nearby.

options.A: Walk to the back room for a mop and warning cone
options.B: Announce the spill over the store's page
options.C: Stand by and signal for help
options.D: Wipe it with paper

explanation: Staying with the hazard keeps shoppers off the slick floor while someone else brings the supplies, which is why safety procedure treats an unattended spill as the thing to prevent first. Walking away for a mop, paging from elsewhere and blotting the oil with paper all leave the puddle uncovered or only partly cleared while customers are in the aisle.

question: A garden center receives a pallet of liquid fertilizer and finds one container leaking onto the dock. The container label warns that the contents irritate skin and eyes, and the product's safety data sheet is filed in the manager's office.

options.A: Wipe the spill up with dry shop towels
options.B: Carry the leaking container across the sales floor to the outside lot to air out
options.C: Keep others away, put on the listed protective gear, and read the sheet
options.D: Wait for the manager to return and unlock the office holding the sheet

explanation: Safety precautions for a chemical spill run in a set order: secure the area, protect yourself with the gear the label calls for, then follow the handling steps the safety data sheet gives for that product. Wiping it up bare-handed exposes skin to a known irritant. Carrying a leaking container spreads the spill along the route. Waiting for the manager leaves an irritant open where employees are working.

question: A cashier at Tanager Goods has forgotten her register code and the line is growing. She asks the coworker beside her to log in with his own code so she can start ringing sales.

options.A: Enter the code and stay beside her while she rings
options.B: Call a manager to unlock the register
options.C: Tell her the register code
options.D: Send customers away

explanation: Register codes tie every transaction to the employee who made it, so restoring access is a manager's job rather than something two cashiers arrange between themselves. Logging her in under his code and telling her the code both break that link, whether or not he stays at the lane, and turning customers away sacrifices sales without addressing the locked register at all.

question: A store's closing procedure requires two employees to be present whenever the day's cash deposit is counted and prepared. One night the assistant manager finds she is the last person in the building.

options.A: Prepare it alone and note the reason
options.B: Leave the deposit in the safe
options.C: Take the deposit to the bank's night drop alone
options.D: Call the bank first

explanation: When the second person required by procedure is unavailable, securing the cash in the safe until two employees are present keeps both the money and the employee protected. Counting it alone breaks the two-person rule that protects her from a later dispute, running a night drop alone adds a personal safety risk, and calling the bank does not supply the second employee the procedure requires.

question: A store-remodel project plan lists a rented scissor lift for the two weeks of ceiling work. Which kind of project resource is the lift?

options.A: An equipment resource for the project
options.B: A human resource for the crew
options.C: A financial resource drawn from the store budget
options.D: A material resource

explanation: Equipment resources are the tools and machines a project uses and returns rather than consumes, which is what a rented lift is. Human resources are the people who do the work, financial resources are the funds that pay for everything, and material resources are the supplies consumed into the finished result.

question: A project manager planning a two-week store reset has confirmed the crew, the fixtures and the budget. Two days out she learns the reset also depends on the fixture vendor's installation software, which the crew has never used and which needs a paid license for each user. How should she treat the software?

options.A: A resource the plan has not yet listed
options.B: A risk to be reviewed once the reset finishes
options.C: A vendor obligation, since the software belongs to the fixture supplier
options.D: A training expense to be charged to the store's payroll budget

explanation: Anything the work cannot proceed without is a project resource, and this one carries both a license cost and a training need that the plan currently accounts for nowhere. Filing it as a risk to review afterward leaves the reset dependent on something unplanned. Calling it the vendor's obligation misreads ownership of the software as ownership of the project's need for it. Booking it as a payroll expense records part of the cost while still leaving the licenses and the crew's inexperience out of the plan.

question: A bottling plant currently learns about underfilled bottles only when a retailer complains weeks after delivery. The plant manager wants those problems found early enough for the line to be corrected the same day. Which quality-control practice does that?

options.A: Sample and measure fill weights throughout the run
options.B: A customer survey
options.C: A monthly sales report by product line
options.D: An annual equipment audit

explanation: Sampling output during the run compares the product against its specification while there is still time to adjust the filler, which is what in-process quality control means. A customer survey and a monthly sales report gather information long after the bottles ship, and an annual audit checks the machine once a year rather than the product being made today.

question: A hotel wants one quality-control measure for the work its housekeeping staff performs. Which of the following is one?

options.A: A monthly staff appreciation lunch
options.B: A redesigned booking website
options.C: Room inspections
options.D: A weekly count of the clean linens held in storage

explanation: Quality control checks finished work against a standard, and inspecting rooms after they are made up does exactly that for housekeeping. An appreciation lunch supports morale, a new booking site serves reservations, and counting linens tracks inventory rather than the condition of the rooms.

question: A print shop rejects 12 percent of finished jobs at final inspection. The rejects trace to one press that drifts out of register partway through long runs. The owner wants fewer rejects without hiring more inspectors.

options.A: Inspect the drifting press's jobs twice
options.B: Add a second final inspection station so fewer flawed jobs reach the customer
options.C: Raise the acceptable register tolerance for long runs
options.D: Check register at set intervals during the run and adjust the press

explanation: Checking during the run catches the drift while paper is still being saved and lets the operator correct the press, which lowers the reject rate instead of measuring it. Inspecting the same jobs twice and adding a second inspection station both find flaws after the sheets are already printed, and each needs the inspection labor the owner ruled out. Loosening the tolerance lowers the reject count by lowering the standard, which passes the drift on to the customer.

question: An associate has to step away from a service-desk terminal that is displaying customer account records. What does data-security practice require of her?

options.A: Lock the screen before walking away
options.B: Turn the monitor so it faces the back counter wall
options.C: Close one window
options.D: Ask a coworker to watch it

explanation: Locking the session means the records cannot be read or used until she signs back in, and it ties whatever happens next to whoever unlocks it. Turning the monitor and closing a single window leave the account still open to anyone who reaches the keyboard, and asking a coworker to watch relies on attention rather than on a control.

question: A store prints a daily pick list that shows customer names, phone numbers and order totals. The sheets are no longer needed once the shift ends. How should staff dispose of them?

options.A: Recycle the paper
options.B: Stack them in the break room for scrap paper use
options.C: File them for a full year
options.D: Shred them before they leave the store

explanation: Paper carrying customer names and phone numbers stays sensitive until it is destroyed, so shredding on site is what keeps the data from being read by anyone who reaches the bin or the truck. Recycling and reusing the sheets as scrap both leave readable records in circulation, and filing them for a year keeps information the store has already finished with.

question: A marketing coordinator wants to analyze customer purchase histories at home this weekend, so she copies the file onto her personal flash drive before leaving. Company policy provides remote access to the same records through a secure company portal.

options.A: Copy the file but delete it from the drive after the weekend
options.B: Password-protect the flash drive file
options.C: Email the file to a personal address instead
options.D: Work through the company portal instead, so the customer file never leaves it

explanation: Using the portal lets her do the same analysis while the customer records stay inside a system the company controls, logs and can revoke. Deleting the copy afterward still leaves the file unprotected on a drive that could be lost all weekend. A password on the file protects the contents but not the decision to carry the records out. Emailing the file to a personal account moves the same data to a second place the company cannot control.

question: A hardware chain counts its entire stock once a year. Between counts the on-hand figures in the point-of-sale system drift far enough that buyers stop trusting them by midsummer. The chain cannot afford to close stores for a second full count.

options.A: Order more of the items the system shows as low
options.B: Have each department manager estimate on-hand quantities at the end of the month
options.C: Move the annual count to early summer
options.D: Cycle count a portion of the items every week during business hours

explanation: Cycle counting keeps records accurate all year by checking a slice of the stock at a time, so no store has to close and errors are corrected as they appear rather than twelve months later. Ordering against figures the buyers already distrust compounds the error. Manager estimates substitute a guess for a count. Moving the annual count changes when the records are accurate without changing how quickly they drift afterward.

question: A stockroom aisle is half blocked by empty pallets and cut steel banding left behind after the morning delivery. Associates are still pulling stock from that aisle. What best maintains a safe work environment?

options.A: Post a sign warning workers about the blocked aisle
options.B: Work around them
options.C: Report it at the next shift meeting
options.D: Clear the aisle right away

explanation: Removing the pallets and banding takes the trip-and-cut hazard out of the aisle, which is what maintaining a safe environment means when the fix is immediate and within the associate's reach. A warning sign leaves the hazard in place, working around it accepts the risk on every trip, and waiting for the next shift meeting delays a correction that takes minutes.

question: A restaurant's back hallway leads to the emergency exit. During a busy week the storeroom fills up, and staff begin stacking cases of bottled drinks along that hallway. What does a safe work environment require?

options.A: Stack them lower
options.B: Label the cases so the staff can move them quickly
options.C: Store them there one week
options.D: Keep the exit route free of the cases

explanation: An exit route has to stay usable in the seconds an emergency allows, so nothing may be stored in it regardless of how neatly it is stacked or how briefly it is meant to sit there. Lower stacks, labels and a one-week limit all still leave obstacles between employees and the door.

question: A grocery's produce department has had three minor slip incidents in one month. All three happened near the misting case in the late afternoon. The department floor is mopped once when the store opens and once at close.

options.A: Add a scheduled floor check during the afternoon hours
options.B: Retrain the produce clerks on the store's slip-and-fall policy
options.C: Place a permanent wet-floor sign beside the misting case so shoppers are warned
options.D: Replace the department's mop heads weekly

explanation: The incidents cluster at a time of day when no one is checking the floor, so putting a check into that gap addresses the actual condition causing the falls. Retraining teaches a policy the clerks are not failing to follow. A permanent sign warns about a hazard the store has chosen to leave on the floor, and shoppers stop noticing signs that are always there. New mop heads improve mopping that is already happening at the wrong hours.

question: While bids are open on a store's rooftop HVAC replacement, one contractor phones the facilities manager with a question about roof access that the written specifications do not address. What should the manager do?

options.A: Answer that one contractor by phone
options.B: Ignore the question
options.C: Answer the question to every bidder in writing
options.D: Extend the bidding deadline

explanation: A fair bid process rests on all bidders pricing the same job from the same information, so an answer that changes the scope has to reach everyone in writing. Answering one caller privately gives that contractor an advantage, ignoring the question leaves a gap in the specifications, and extending the deadline gives more time without supplying the missing information.

question: Four sealed bids arrive for a warehouse racking installation. The lowest is 30 percent under the other three, and its scope sheet leaves out the seismic bracing the specification requires. The bid deadline has already passed.

options.A: Award the lowest bid and add bracing later
options.B: Reject the incomplete bid and award among the three conforming ones
options.C: Reopen the bidding for all four contractors
options.D: Let the low bidder submit a revised price that includes the seismic bracing

explanation: A bid that omits required scope is not a bid for the job that was advertised, and setting it aside protects both the specification and the three contractors who priced the work in full. Awarding it and adding bracing afterward hands that contractor a change order at prices nobody competed on. Reopening bidding penalizes the compliant bidders for someone else's omission. Allowing a revised price after the deadline lets one bidder price the job knowing the others' terms.

question: When a supervisor hands a multi-week assignment to an employee, what makes it possible to follow the work later without standing over the employee?

options.A: A daily written progress email
options.B: A weekly bonus offer
options.C: A copy of the supervisor's own working checklist
options.D: Agreed milestones set at the handoff

explanation: Milestones agreed when the work is handed over give both people the same markers to measure against, so progress can be judged at set points instead of by constant observation. A daily email demands attention every day whether or not anything has changed, a bonus rewards the outcome without revealing progress, and handing over the supervisor's own checklist dictates method rather than tracking results.

question: A supervisor delegated the quarterly vendor-compliance file to an experienced coordinator, due Friday. At the midpoint check she reports she is on track, but the draft she shares is missing two of the vendors the file must cover.

options.A: Complete the two missing vendor entries himself so Friday's deadline is protected
options.B: Raise the two missing vendors with her
options.C: Wait until Friday and review the finished file
options.D: Move the deadline back a week to give her more working time

explanation: Monitoring works by feeding what the supervisor observes back to the person doing the task while there is still time to act on it. Filling in the entries himself takes the assignment back and teaches nothing. Waiting until Friday wastes the very check-in that surfaced the gap. Moving the deadline treats a two-vendor omission as a schedule problem when the coordinator may simply have a different list.

question: A project manager reads the weekly report for a store remodel and sees that 40 percent of the budget is spent while 20 percent of the work is finished. What does monitoring call for now?

options.A: Wait one more week
options.B: Ask the crew to add unpaid hours to catch the budget
options.C: Correct the plan before more is spent
options.D: Record the figures and move on

explanation: Monitoring exists to trigger correction, and spending that is running at twice the rate of progress is exactly the signal a plan needs to be reworked before the remaining budget follows it. Waiting a week and simply filing the figures both let the overspend continue, and asking a crew to work unpaid hours shifts the cost onto employees instead of fixing the plan.

question: Six weeks into a ten-week product photo shoot, the weekly report shows the photographer producing 60 images a week against a plan of 100. The finished images feed a fall catalog whose printing date cannot move.

options.A: Extend the shoot schedule by four weeks
options.B: Keep the current pace and report the shortfall in the final project summary
options.C: Add photographer hours now to close the weekly gap
options.D: Reprint the catalog later with the missing product images

explanation: With the deadline fixed and four weeks left, the only correction that still delivers the catalog is adding capacity now, while the remaining gap is small enough to close. Extending the schedule breaks the printing date the project exists to meet. Reporting the shortfall at the end is monitoring without correction. A second printing pays twice for one catalog and delivers the images after the season they were shot for.

question: An office coordinator's morning list holds twelve small errands, and most of them use either the shared copier or the shipping station at the other end of the floor. None of them is urgent. Which approach saves the most time?

options.A: Group the like tasks together
options.B: Handle each task as the request arrives by email
options.C: Start with the shortest task first
options.D: Work alphabetically

explanation: Batching tasks that use the same equipment removes the walking and setup repeated on every separate trip, which is where the time in this list is going. Working from the inbox lets arrival order drive the day, shortest-first ignores which station each task needs, and alphabetical order is unrelated to the work itself.

question: At nine o'clock a store manager faces four things: the payroll file due to corporate at noon, a customer complaint escalated to her overnight, a vendor representative waiting in her office without an appointment, and a floor reset she had blocked out for today. What should she do first?

options.A: Meet the waiting vendor rep before anything else
options.B: File payroll first, since the noon deadline affects every employee
options.C: Start the floor reset while the morning is quiet and the crew is available
options.D: Answer the escalated complaint first

explanation: Prioritizing weighs urgency against consequence, and payroll is the only item with a hard deadline three hours away whose failure would hit the whole staff. The unannounced vendor sets the manager's agenda by arriving. The floor reset is important but has all day and belongs to the crew. The complaint deserves a response today, and it will still be answerable at noon, while payroll will not.

question: A store's shelf of its top-moving cleaner is nearly empty, and the supplier's next truck is five days out. What does the associate most need to know before placing the reorder?

options.A: How many cases sell over a five-day delivery wait
options.B: The item's shelf tag
options.C: Last year's total sales for the store
options.D: The supplier's street address

explanation: The order has to cover demand until the delivery lands, so sales during the supplier's lead time is the figure that decides both whether to order now and how much. The shelf tag gives price and location, last year's store total is far too broad to size one item's order, and the supplier's address is administrative detail the store already has on file.

question: A buyer wants the system to generate an order automatically whenever the stock of a staple item drops to a set level. Which figure must be stored for the item?

options.A: The item's current retail price tag
options.B: The item's set reorder point
options.C: The supplier's total sales for the past two years
options.D: The store's hours

explanation: The reorder point is the stock level at which replenishment is triggered, so it is the number the system compares the on-hand count against. Retail price affects margin rather than timing, the supplier's own sales history says nothing about this store's stock level, and store hours have no bearing on when stock runs low.

question: A cafe sells twenty pounds of espresso beans a week. Its roaster takes two weeks to deliver, and the cafe keeps one week of beans as a cushion. The manager sees forty-five pounds on hand, and the roaster has announced a price increase that starts in thirty days.

options.A: Buy an extra three months of beans now so the coming price increase is avoided
options.B: Place the reorder with the roaster today
options.C: Wait until the last few pounds remain to order
options.D: Switch to a roaster with a shorter delivery time

explanation: Two weeks of lead time plus a one-week cushion means the cafe should reorder while sixty pounds remain, and forty-five is already below that, so the order is due today. Buying three months of beans ties up cash and risks stale coffee to dodge a price change. Waiting for the last few pounds guarantees a stockout during the two-week wait. Changing roasters is a sourcing decision that does nothing about the beans running out this month.

question: A manager has agreed the goals for a store's back-office renovation and now needs to know how long the work will run and how many people are needed each week. Which planning step produces that?

options.A: Draft the final project report early
options.B: Sign the contract
options.C: Break the work into tasks and estimate each one
options.D: Order the materials early

explanation: Duration and staffing come out of decomposing the work and estimating the pieces, because a schedule can only be built once the tasks and their sizes are known. A final report closes the project, a signed contract commits money before the scope is sized, and ordering materials early spends the budget on estimates nobody has made yet.

question: A regional manager is planning a two-month rollout of new checkout software across 18 stores. Two of those stores are already booked for remodels inside that window, and the district's only trainer is on leave for three weeks in the middle of it.

options.A: Roll out to all 18 stores in one week
options.B: Ask each store manager to train their own team from the vendor's online modules
options.C: Build the schedule around the trainer's leave and the two remodels
options.D: Delay the entire rollout until after the remodels

explanation: Planning means fitting the work to the constraints that are already known, and both the trainer's leave and the remodel dates are fixed facts the schedule can be shaped around. A one-week rollout ignores the trainer constraint entirely. Pushing training onto store managers drops the quality the trainer exists to provide. Delaying everything treats two stores' remodels as a reason to hold up the other sixteen.
